lede: A drawing teacher's son from Malaga whose father, by family legend, handed him his own brushes when he was a boy, and who spent more than seventy years breaking every rule of how a picture should look and became the most famous artist of the 20th century.

ps: Pablo Ruiz Picasso was born in Malaga, in southern Spain, on 25 October 1881. He trained in Barcelona and from 1904 lived in France for the rest of his life.

With Georges Braque he invented Cubism, which broke objects into facets seen from several sides at once. In 1937 he painted Guernica, a vast black-and-white protest against the bombing of a Basque town in the Spanish Civil War.
He made paintings, sculpture, prints, ceramics and stage designs, perhaps tens of thousands of works in all. He died at Mougins, near Cannes, on 8 April 1973, aged 91.
His father, Jose Ruiz Blasco, was a painter of birds and an art teacher. Pablo drew before he could talk well, and the family later said his first word was 'piz', for lapiz, pencil.
The family moved to A Coruna in 1891 and to Barcelona in 1895, where his father taught at the art school, La Llotja. Pablo, aged 13 or 14, was admitted to its advanced classes.

ps.t: His father, it is said, saw his son's skill and gave up painting himself, handing Pablo his brushes.
ps.why: A family story told later by Picasso himself; there is no independent record.

ps: In 1895 his younger sister Conchita died of diphtheria. He went briefly to the Royal Academy in Madrid in 1897, found it dull, and returned to Barcelona, where he met young writers and artists at the cafe Els Quatre Gats.

1900 to 1901: he first visited Paris with his friend Carles Casagemas. In February 1901 Casagemas shot himself in a Paris cafe. Picasso's grief led into the Blue Period, years of cold blue pictures of beggars, the blind and the poor.
1904: he settled in Montmartre in a ramshackle studio building called the Bateau-Lavoir, and lived with Fernande Olivier. His colours warmed into the Rose Period of circus performers and acrobats.
1905 to 1906: he painted a portrait of the writer Gertrude Stein, who said it did not look like her. He is said to have replied that it would.

1907: he painted Les Demoiselles d'Avignon, five naked women with mask-like faces, influenced by ancient Iberian sculpture and African masks he saw at the Trocadero museum. Even his friends were shocked. It was hardly seen in public until 1916.

1908 to 1914: he and Georges Braque worked so closely, Braque said, that they were like two mountaineers roped together. Together they created Cubism, then collage, gluing real things like oilcloth and newspaper into pictures.
1917 to 1918: he designed sets and costumes for Sergei Diaghilev's Ballets Russes, and married the dancer Olga Khokhlova. Their son Paulo was born in 1921.

1937: on 26 April German and Italian aircraft, supporting Franco's Nationalists, bombed the Basque town of Guernica on a market day. Picasso, commissioned by the Spanish Republic to make a mural for its pavilion at the Paris World's Fair, painted Guernica in about five weeks.

1940 to 1944: he stayed in occupied Paris. He was banned from exhibiting, but kept working in his studio on the rue des Grands-Augustins. In October 1944, after liberation, he joined the French Communist Party.
1946 to 1955: in the south of France he made ceramics at the Madoura pottery in Vallauris. His lithograph of a dove became the emblem of the 1949 Paris Peace Congress.
1961: he married Jacqueline Roque. They lived at Mougins, where he worked almost to the day he died.
The Old Guitarist (about 1903). A Blue Period picture of a thin, bent, blind man playing in the street.
Les Demoiselles d'Avignon (1907). Now at the Museum of Modern Art in New York, often called the first truly modern painting.

Guernica (1937). About 3.5 metres high and almost 8 metres long, in black, white and grey: a screaming mother with a dead child, a bull, a wounded horse, a fallen soldier with a broken sword, a woman reaching out with a lamp. Picasso asked that it not go to Spain until democracy returned. It arrived in 1981, and since 1992 has hung in the Museo Reina Sofia in Madrid.
Bull's Head (1942). A sculpture made from nothing but a bicycle seat and handlebars, later cast in bronze.
He also made hundreds of prints, including the Vollard Suite of the 1930s, and thousands of ceramic plates, jugs and figures.
Georges Braque (1882 to 1963), his partner in Cubism. They drifted apart after Braque went to war in 1914.
Henri Matisse (1869 to 1954), his great rival. Each watched what the other did for half a century.
Paul Cezanne (1839 to 1906), the older painter whose way of building forms from planes helped lead to Cubism.
Gertrude Stein (1874 to 1946), the American writer and collector, an early supporter.
Guillaume Apollinaire (1880 to 1918), the poet and critic, his close friend in Montmartre.

The women in his life were also his models: Fernande Olivier, Olga Khokhlova, Marie-Therese Walter (mother of his daughter Maya, born 1935), Dora Maar, Francoise Gilot (mother of Claude and Paloma) and Jacqueline Roque.
He lived through two world wars, the Spanish Civil War and the Cold War. Spain was ruled by General Franco from 1939 until 1975, and Picasso never went back.
Paris in the early 1900s drew artists from everywhere, and dealers such as Ambroise Vollard and Daniel-Henry Kahnweiler built markets for work that the official salons rejected.
Few artists have changed so many kinds of art. Cubism opened the way for abstraction, and collage and assemblage, art made from found things, became basic tools of modern artists.

ps.t: His treatment of the women close to him is now part of how he is judged. He met Marie-Therese Walter when she was 17 and he was 45. Dora Maar, an artist and photographer who recorded the making of Guernica, had a breakdown after their relationship ended. Francoise Gilot, who left him in 1953, described his controlling and cruel behaviour in her book Life with Picasso (1964).
ps.why: Dates are documented; descriptions of his behaviour come mainly from Gilot and others close to him, and are widely accepted by biographers.

ps: Museums devoted to him include the Museu Picasso in Barcelona, opened in 1963, the Musee Picasso in Paris, opened in 1985 with works his heirs gave the French state to settle inheritance taxes, and the Museo Picasso Malaga.

myths.c: A German officer saw Guernica and asked, 'Did you do this?' Picasso answered, 'No, you did.'
myths.t: The story is told in many versions, sometimes about a photograph or postcard of the painting in occupied Paris. There is no first-hand record, and it may be a legend.

myths.c: As a boy he painted like Raphael.
myths.t: Picasso is quoted as saying he drew like Raphael as a child and spent a lifetime learning to draw like a child. His teenage academic studies are skilled, but the line was part of the legend he built about himself.

When the Mona Lisa was stolen in 1911, the police questioned him and arrested his friend Apollinaire, because both were linked to small Iberian statues that a friend had stolen from the Louvre earlier and that Picasso had bought. They had nothing to do with the Mona Lisa. A museum worker, Vincenzo Peruggia, had taken it.

myths.c: He was the richest artist who ever lived.
myths.t: He left an enormous estate, including tens of thousands of his own works. His wealth came from a very long, productive life and from strong demand while he was still alive, which is rare for artists.
